Seen in this light, the intellectual forms taken by the party conflicts at the end of the Rightly Guided period had not yet reached the stage of relative independence we are describing.

For example, most of the intellectual debate between the three main parties during the lifetime of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib still revolved around religious texts and their interpretation.

Thinking about these questions gradually moved from being closely tied to the wording of texts toward examining the questions themselves more deeply, and only then returning to the texts as support for rational argument and as evidence that the reasoning was sound.

In this way, debate moved from treating these issues mainly as questions of law to treating them as questions of religion itself.

The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

To sum up this chapter: the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs came to an end before the intellectual forms of the social and political conflicts of that period had fully undergone this development.

The chapter begins with the Prophet’s death in 632 CE, twenty-two years after he began preaching Islam. His death created two different kinds of confusion among Muslims, each touching on the social, political, and religious meaning of Islam.

One group of Muslims could not believe that the Prophet had died. They understood his prophethood in a way that placed him outside the ordinary conditions of human life, and so they imagined that he could not die. Abu Bakr brought this confusion to a decisive end. He reminded people of the Prophet’s humanity and supported his argument with Qurʾanic verses stating that Muhammad was human.

Another group of Muslims was shocked by the Prophet’s permanent disappearance from his position as leader of the Islamic community. They did not know what would happen to that position after his death.
The chapter then follows the conflicts that developed around this position of leadership and the different forms they took.

As soon as the Prophet’s death was announced, old tensions that had previously been held in check suddenly broke into the open. There were tensions between Mecca and Medina, then between the Emigrants and the Helpers, then among the Emigrants themselves between the Hāshimites and non-Hāshimites, and finally between the Aws and Khazraj among the Helpers. All of this erupted while the Prophet’s body was still in the home of his wife ʿĀʾisha, before he had even been buried.

The struggle for power now came openly to the surface among all these groups. Their motives became clear in the meeting they immediately held at the Saqīfa of Banū Sāʿida to decide who would succeed the Prophet.

Although one of the leaders of the Helpers, Abu ʿUbayda ibn al-Jarrāḥ, settled the immediate dispute by pledging allegiance to Abu Bakr as the Prophet’s first caliph, the matter was not settled historically or religiously. From that moment, the first seeds appeared of political and sectarian factionalism within Islam. These divisions continued to grow as events unfolded, and they produced their first major results before the age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs had even come to an end.
We describe this factionalism as both political and sectarian because the political struggle over the caliphate soon took on the form of a religious dispute over what the caliphate itself meant.
One side held that the caliphate was a divinely appointed office. God, through the Prophet, had designated the person who should hold it. These were the supporters of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib.
The other side held that the caliphate was an office whose holder should be chosen by Muslims because they considered him fit for it.

This second group wanted the caliph to be selected through what became known as the principle of shūrā, meaning consultation among Muslims in choosing a leader. In practice, however, the selection of the four Rightly Guided Caliphs involved little more than a narrow and largely formal version of this principle.

At one point, the choice rested with a single individual, as when Abu Bakr chose ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb to succeed him. At another, it was confined to only a handful of people, no more than four at most, as happened when the third caliph, ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, was appointed.

We therefore concluded that the principle of shūrā never acquired a clear legal or practical form in Islam, not even during what is usually regarded as the most “democratic” period of the caliphate: the age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs.

Among the reactions that followed the Prophet’s death, the chapter also discusses the decision by many people in regions far from Mecca and Medina—including al-Yamāma, Yemen, Hadramawt, Oman, and elsewhere—to renounce their allegiance to Islam.
The new caliph, Abu Bakr, sent military forces against them in the conflicts known in Islamic history as the Ridda Wars, or Wars of Apostasy.
We discussed several reasons for these rebellions.
Some tribes had never fully accepted Islamic rule because their chiefs saw no advantage in accepting Islam’s attempt to break down the older framework of tribal unity.
Other tribes had outwardly submitted because Islam had become the strongest political center in Arabia after the conquest of Mecca.

The settled agricultural regions were in a different position. Their existing systems of production gave them reasons to preserve their established traditions and social arrangements rather than accept changes they did not need.

These regions also produced people who claimed prophethood for themselves. Such figures naturally opposed submission to Muhammad’s message and teachings. Among them were Musaylima of Banū Ḥanīfa in al-Yamāma and the woman Sajāḥ among Banū Taghlib.

When Muhammad died, all these groups saw an opportunity to rise against Islamic rule. The military campaigns sent against them by the caliphs succeeded, however, and the rebels were brought back under the authority of the caliphate.
The chapter also discusses the Islamic conquests beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

We saw that Arab expansion began only a year after the Prophet’s death. Its first direction was toward Syria and Palestine, which were then under Byzantine rule. The conquests continued for more than seventy years, until the Arab state stretched across vast areas of three continents.

The historical evidence led us to conclude that the main driving forces behind this movement were social rather than religious. For this reason, we rejected the view of some Orientalist scholars that religious fanaticism was what drove the Arab conquests.

Looking at the conditions in which the wars were fought and the victories won by the Arab armies, we concluded that success depended both on conditions within the conquered countries and on conditions among the conquerors themselves.

Among the conditions in the conquered lands was the weakness of the Byzantine and Persian states after their long wars against one another. The populations of Syria, Palestine, Egypt, and Iraq were also burdened by heavy taxation. In Syria, they faced religious persecution from the Byzantine Church as well.

On the Arab side, the conquerors did not initially rule the peoples of these countries through the feudal system used by their previous rulers, because the Arabs themselves had not practiced this kind of government before the conquests.

The Arab conquerors also followed a policy of religious tolerance. They did not plunder the cities they conquered, though they did confiscate the property of the wealthy and the nobility. Nor did they take land away from its existing owners until the reign of the third Rightly Guided Caliph, ʿUthmān.
The policies followed by the Arab conquerors also allowed us to draw several further conclusions.

One was that their religious tolerance had a material basis. They had an interest in limiting the number of Christians who converted to Islam so that revenue from the jizya, the tax imposed on non-Muslims, would not fall.

Another was their favorable treatment of local Christian clergy. These clergy had opposed the Byzantine church authorities, and that religious opposition also carried a political meaning: resistance to the rule of a foreign occupying power, Byzantium.
We also concluded that the Arab conquerors did not change the existing division of labor among the local population.

We noted that the cultural and social interaction between the Arabs and the peoples of the conquered countries did not yet show its full effects during the age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs. Those effects became much clearer later.

We concluded that this interaction was delayed mainly because, during the early period of conquest, the conquerors lived separately from the local population. They were occupied with military defense and the organization of their armies, and they did not take part in material production.
For this reason, we rejected the claim made by some modern researchers that the Arabs rejected the cultures of these peoples.

The issue was not rejection. It was the particular conditions in which the conquerors were living. Those conditions delayed cultural interaction for a time. Once they changed, the process developed with tremendous force.

We also noted that the conditions created by the conquests opened the way for a new kind of intellectual activity in Islamic law: independent legal reasoning based on personal judgment, or ijtihād bi-l-raʾy.
This movement had a positive role in the development of Islamic law.
The second caliph, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, practiced this kind of personal reasoning with both boldness and foresight.

We concluded that the appearance of this method shows Arab thought beginning to move in a new direction. After the age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, it would enter a different intellectual climate, one closer to rational inquiry.
Thought would then begin to examine the doctrines of faith themselves, as we shall see.
The conclusions we have drawn about the Arab conquests and Arab policy in the conquered lands apply only to the earliest period of expansion.
Later, we saw major changes in the relationship between the Arabs and the local populations.

One development during the age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs is especially striking. Under the third caliph, ʿUthmān, a semi-feudal aristocratic “class” began to form among the Umayyad governors whom he appointed from among his own relatives.
These governors pursued personal enrichment, accumulated land, and burdened the population with taxes. In doing so, they created the conditions for a social uprising in the conquered provinces.
That uprising eventually led to the killing of the caliph himself.

It also produced a new factional struggle that reached the point of armed conflict between the fourth caliph, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, and Muʿāwiya, the governor of Syria and representative of the Umayyad party.
A new party also emerged from ʿAlī’s own ranks during the Battle of Ṣiffīn: the Kharijites.
